title: Stage IV Grade C Periodontitis in a Poorly Controlled Diabetic Smoker — Staging, Sequencing & Risk Modification
short: 52M • T2DM HbA1c 9.2% • 1 PPD smoker • Generalized Stage IV Grade C

patient.medical_history: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (HbA1c 9.2%, on metformin + glipizide), hypertension (lisinopril), 20 pack-year smoking history (currently 1 PPD). No known drug allergies. Last medical visit 8 months ago.
patient.chief_complaint: My gums bleed when I brush and several teeth feel loose. I was told years ago I have gum disease but never followed through.

clinical_findings.probing_depths: Generalized 5–9 mm PDs with 70% BOP. Interproximal CAL ≥5 mm on ≥30% of teeth. Vertical bone loss to mid-root on multiple posterior teeth. #3, #14, #19, #30 exhibit Class II–III furcation involvement. Pathologic migration of #8 and #9 with diastema formation. 4 teeth with mobility ≥2.
clinical_findings.radiographs: Full-mouth series + panoramic: generalized horizontal bone loss 50–70%, angular defects on #3, #14, #19, #30. No endodontic pathology. Crestal bone levels consistent with Stage IV.

flags: Multiple hopeless teeth + strategic abutment decisions
guidelines: 2018 AAP/EFP Classification of Periodontal and Peri-Implant Diseases
2017 World Workshop on the Classification of Periodontal and Peri-Implant Diseases and Conditions
S3-level clinical practice guideline for treatment of Stage I–III periodontitis (EFP 2020) and Stage IV (EFP 2022)

vignette.demographics: 52-year-old male, ASA III. Type 2 DM with HbA1c 9.2%, hypertension, current 1 PPD smoker (20 pack-years). Poorly compliant with medical and dental care.
vignette.chief: Progressive gingival bleeding, tooth mobility, and shifting of anterior teeth. Patient reports no professional care for >6 years.
vignette.clinical: Generalized plaque and calculus. PDs 5–9 mm with 70% BOP. Interdental CAL ≥5 mm affecting >30% of sites. Pathologic migration of maxillary incisors. Class II–III furcations on all first molars. Multiple teeth with Grade 2 mobility. Thin periodontal phenotype in the anterior.
vignette.endo: All teeth vital except #30 (previous RCT, asymptomatic, no apical radiolucency). No sinus tracts.
vignette.radio: Generalized moderate-to-severe horizontal bone loss with vertical components on molars. Furcation arrows positive. Remaining periodontal support <30% on several strategic teeth. No obvious caries or periapical lesions.

questions.q: According to the 2018 AAP/EFP classification, what is the correct Stage and Grade for this patient, and which single finding most strongly drives the Grade assignment?
options: Stage III Grade B — driven by the amount of bone loss relative to age
Stage IV Grade C — driven by the combination of rapid progression evidence, smoking ≥10 cigarettes/day, and uncontrolled diabetes
Stage IV Grade B — driven only by the need for complex rehabilitation
Stage III Grade C — driven by CAL ≥5 mm and furcation involvement
questions.explanation: Stage is determined by severity and complexity. CAL ≥5 mm, bone loss extending to mid-root, furcation involvement, and the need for complex rehabilitation (pathologic migration, multiple missing/hopeless teeth, bite collapse risk) place the patient in Stage IV. Grade reflects progression rate and risk factors. Grade C is assigned when there is evidence of rapid progression or when grade modifiers (smoking ≥10 cigarettes/day and/or HbA1c ≥7.0%) are present. Here both modifiers are strongly positive, confirming Grade C. Stage III would lack the complexity features; Grade B would under-weight the risk factor profile.

questions.q: Which initial therapy sequence is most evidence-based and guideline-concordant before any surgical or implant decisions?
options: Immediate extraction of all Grade 2 mobile teeth, followed by implant-supported fixed rehabilitation once HbA1c is <8%

Non-surgical periodontal therapy (step 1–2 of EFP S3 guideline) + smoking cessation counseling + physician-coordinated glycemic optimization, with re-evaluation at 8–12 weeks before any surgical intervention
Systemic amoxicillin/metronidazole for 7 days followed by immediate regenerative surgery on angular defects
Host-modulation with low-dose doxycycline as monotherapy while the patient continues smoking
questions.explanation: EFP S3 clinical practice guidelines (2020/2022) mandate a stepwise approach. Steps 1–2 (behavioral change, risk-factor control, supra- and subgingival instrumentation) must precede surgical therapy. Uncontrolled diabetes and ongoing smoking significantly impair wound healing and increase progressive attachment loss; both must be addressed concurrently. Re-evaluation at 8–12 weeks determines residual disease and candidacy for step 3 (surgical) therapy. Immediate extractions or regenerative surgery without risk-factor control violate the evidence hierarchy and increase the risk of early implant or regenerative failure. Systemic antibiotics are adjunctive only in specific microbiological situations and never replace mechanical therapy and risk-factor modification. Low-dose doxycycline monotherapy is insufficient.

questions.q: After successful non-surgical therapy and risk-factor reduction (HbA1c now 7.1%, smoking reduced to <5 cigarettes/day), which residual site is the strongest candidate for regenerative periodontal surgery rather than extraction + implant?
options: #19 with Class III furcation, 9 mm PD, and <1/3 remaining bone support
Mandibular anterior teeth with horizontal bone loss and 5 mm residual PDs
A deep, narrow 2–3 wall intrabony defect on the mesial of #20 with 7 mm residual PD and thick phenotype after non-surgical therapy
Any site with Grade 2 mobility regardless of defect morphology
questions.explanation: Regenerative therapy has the highest predictability in deep, narrow intrabony defects (preferably 2–3 wall) with adequate containment and thick soft-tissue phenotype. Class III furcations and teeth with <30% remaining bone support have poor regenerative prognosis and are often better managed by extraction and implant therapy once systemic risks are controlled. Horizontal defects respond poorly to regeneration. Mobility alone does not contraindicate regeneration if the defect morphology is favorable and occlusal trauma is controlled. The EFP and AAP literature consistently identify defect morphology and residual containment as the dominant predictors of regenerative success.

title: Progressive Peri-Implantitis at a Mandibular Molar Implant — Diagnosis, Non-Surgical Limits & Explantation Threshold
short: 48F • #19 implant • 4.5 mm bone loss • BOP + suppuration • History of periodontitis

patient.medical_history: Former smoker (quit 6 years ago), history of Stage III periodontitis treated 9 years earlier. No diabetes. Takes atorvastatin and a multivitamin. NKDA.
patient.chief_complaint: My back implant tooth feels tender when I chew and the gum around it bleeds and tastes bad.

clinical_findings.probing_depths: #19 implant: PD 7–8 mm with BOP and frank suppuration on probing. Keratinized mucosa 1 mm on buccal. Adjacent natural teeth stable (PD ≤4 mm, no BOP).
clinical_findings.mobility: Implant is non-mobile. No prosthetic complications (screw-retained zirconia crown, no occlusal prematurity).
clinical_findings.radiographs: Periapical + CBCT: vertical bone loss of 4.5 mm from the implant platform on mesial and distal, crater-like morphology, no implant fracture or loss of integration at apex. Buccal plate thinned but intact.

flags: History of periodontitis (strongest risk factor for peri-implantitis)
Progressive radiographic bone loss >3 mm + BOP/suppuration
guidelines: 2017 World Workshop on the Classification of Periodontal and Peri-Implant Diseases and Conditions
2018 AAP/EFP Peri-implantitis case definitions
ITI Treatment Guide Vol. 11 & current consensus on peri-implantitis management

vignette.demographics: 48-year-old female, ASA II. History of Stage III periodontitis, former smoker. #19 replaced with bone-level implant and screw-retained crown 7 years ago. Regular maintenance until 18 months ago.
vignette.chief: Localized tenderness on mastication, bleeding, and bad taste associated with the implant at #19.
vignette.clinical: PD 7–8 mm around #19 implant with BOP and suppuration. Minimal keratinized tissue (≤1 mm). No mobility. Soft-tissue erythema and slight edema. Adjacent periodontium healthy.
vignette.endo: Not applicable (implant). Crown margins appear closed; no residual cement visible clinically.
vignette.radio: CBCT confirms 4.5 mm vertical bone loss from platform, crater morphology, implant surface exposure, no apical involvement or fracture. Remaining bone support approximately 50% of implant length.

questions.q: Using the 2017/2018 World Workshop case definition, does this implant meet criteria for peri-implantitis, and which finding is required for the diagnosis in the presence of prior radiographs?
options: No — bone loss <6 mm excludes peri-implantitis
Yes — presence of BOP/suppuration + progressive bone loss beyond normal remodeling (here 4.5 mm) meets the case definition
No — absence of implant mobility rules out peri-implantitis
Yes — but only if PD ≥8 mm; 7 mm is still peri-implant mucositis
questions.explanation: The 2017 World Workshop defines peri-implantitis as a pathological condition occurring in tissues around dental implants, characterized by inflammation in the peri-implant mucosa and progressive loss of supporting bone. In the presence of baseline radiographs, progressive bone loss is the key discriminator from peri-implant mucositis. BOP or suppuration indicates inflammation. There is no absolute bone-loss millimeter threshold once progression is documented; 4.5 mm clearly exceeds expected remodeling. Mobility indicates end-stage loss of osseointegration and is not required for the diagnosis of peri-implantitis. PD alone does not define the disease when inflammation and progressive bone loss are present.

questions.q: What is the most evidence-supported next step after confirming the diagnosis and removing the prosthesis for access?
options: Non-surgical mechanical debridement + local antibiotics alone, with expectation of full bony regeneration

Open-flap debridement with surface decontamination, possible implantoplasty or resective recontouring, and apical positioning or soft-tissue grafting to improve cleansability, followed by strict maintenance; explantation if residual deep PD and continued progression
Immediate explantation and simultaneous GBR + delayed implant replacement
Systemic antibiotics for 14 days without mechanical intervention
questions.explanation: Current consensus (ITI, EFP, AAP) holds that non-surgical therapy alone has limited efficacy once progressive bone loss and crater defects are established, especially with limited keratinized mucosa. Surgical access allows thorough surface decontamination, defect assessment, and soft-tissue management. Implantoplasty or resective approaches can improve cleansability in non-esthetic zones. Regeneration remains unpredictable on previously contaminated implant surfaces. Explantation is reserved for advanced bone loss, mobility, or failure to control inflammation after surgical therapy. Systemic antibiotics without mechanical debridement are ineffective. The stepwise philosophy mirrors periodontitis management: control inflammation and create a maintainable environment before considering removal.

questions.q: Which patient-level factor most strongly predicts recurrence or progression of peri-implantitis after therapy?
options: History of periodontitis and residual periodontal pockets elsewhere in the mouth
Choice of implant surface (rough vs machined)
Age of the patient
Whether the crown was cement- or screw-retained
questions.explanation: A history of periodontitis is the strongest and most consistently reported patient-level risk factor for both incidence and progression of peri-implantitis. Residual deep pockets serve as a reservoir for periopathogens that can colonize implants. While implant surface characteristics and prosthetic design influence local plaque retention, they are secondary to the patient’s susceptibility profile. Age itself is not an independent predictor once periodontal history and maintenance compliance are accounted for. Ongoing supportive peri-implant care and control of residual periodontitis are therefore mandatory components of any treatment plan.

title: Vertical and Horizontal Ridge Deficiency in the Esthetic Zone — Staged Soft- and Hard-Tissue Reconstruction
short: 35F • #9 avulsed 4 yrs ago • Thin phenotype • Seibert Class III defect

patient.medical_history: Healthy, non-smoker, no medications, NKDA. High esthetic demand; works in media.
patient.chief_complaint: I lost my front tooth years ago in an accident and the temporary flipper looks unnatural. I want a permanent implant that looks like a real tooth.

clinical_findings.probing_depths: Adjacent teeth #8 and #10: PD 2–3 mm, no BOP, thick biotype on #8 but thin scalloped phenotype at edentulous site. Mid-crestal soft-tissue deficiency of 3–4 mm vertically relative to adjacent CEJs. Horizontal collapse with loss of buccal convexity.
clinical_findings.radiographs: CBCT: residual ridge width 3.5 mm at crest, vertical bone deficiency of approximately 4 mm relative to ideal implant position. Facial plate absent in the coronal third. Adequate apical bone for implant anchorage after reconstruction.

flags: Seibert Class III (combined horizontal + vertical) defect
guidelines: ITI Treatment Guides (esthetic zone, bone augmentation)
2017 World Workshop — peri-implant soft-tissue considerations
Current evidence on staged vs simultaneous GBR in the anterior maxilla

vignette.demographics: 35-year-old healthy non-smoking female with high esthetic expectations. #9 lost to trauma 4 years earlier; site left unrestored except for a removable flipper.
vignette.chief: Desire for a fixed, natural-appearing replacement of #9. Dissatisfied with the appearance of the removable prosthesis and the collapsed ridge.
vignette.clinical: Edentulous ridge #9 with vertical soft-tissue deficiency of 3–4 mm and significant buccal collapse. Thin scalloped phenotype. Adjacent teeth periodontally healthy with differential biotype. High smile line exposing the entire site.
vignette.radio: CBCT demonstrates knife-edge ridge (3.5 mm crestal width), 4 mm vertical deficiency, and missing facial plate in the coronal 4–5 mm. Apical bone volume sufficient once the ridge is reconstructed.

questions.q: What is the most predictable overall treatment sequence for achieving both hard- and soft-tissue volume compatible with a high esthetic implant result?
options: Immediate implant placement with simultaneous particulate grafting and connective-tissue graft

Staged approach: horizontal and vertical bone augmentation (preferably with space-maintaining technique) first, followed by soft-tissue augmentation after graft maturation, then implant placement in a prosthetically driven position
Soft-tissue grafting alone followed by narrow-diameter implant placement
Extraction of #8 and #10 and placement of a three-unit implant-supported bridge to avoid ridge augmentation
questions.explanation: Long-standing Seibert Class III defects in the esthetic zone rarely allow simultaneous implant placement with predictable pink-and-white outcomes. Staged reconstruction permits (1) restoration of bone volume and contours under optimized healing conditions, (2) subsequent soft-tissue thickening and apical positioning of the mucogingival junction, and (3) prosthetically driven implant placement into a reconstructed ridge. Immediate placement into a deficient, long-healed site risks malposition, recession, and soft-tissue dehiscence. Soft-tissue grafting alone cannot restore the missing bone housing. Sacrificing adjacent healthy teeth is not justified when site development is feasible.

questions.q: Which combination of materials and technique has the strongest current evidence for simultaneous horizontal + vertical augmentation in this defect morphology?
options: Particulate xenograft alone under a resorbable collagen membrane (GBR) without space maintenance
Autogenous block graft (e.g., ramus or symphysis) or titanium-reinforced membrane / mesh with particulate graft to maintain space, plus primary passive closure
Allograft putty injected through a tunneling approach
rhBMP-2 alone without scaffolding or membrane
questions.explanation: Vertical augmentation remains more technique-sensitive than horizontal. Space maintenance is critical; particulate grafts under non-reinforced resorbable membranes tend to collapse under soft-tissue pressure. Autogenous blocks or reinforced barrier techniques (titanium mesh, reinforced e-PTFE, or similar) provide the necessary resistance to compression and have the most robust data for combined defects. Passive primary closure is mandatory to avoid exposure and graft failure. Tunnel approaches and putties lack the volumetric stability required for 4 mm vertical gain. rhBMP-2 can be an adjunct but still requires a scaffold and space-maintaining strategy.

questions.q: After successful bone augmentation and implant placement, which soft-tissue parameter is most critical to long-term esthetic stability and peri-implant health at this site?
options: Presence of at least 2 mm of keratinized mucosa and adequate soft-tissue thickness (≥2 mm) on the buccal aspect
Complete elimination of all probing depths around the implant
Use of a stock titanium abutment rather than a custom zirconia abutment
Avoidance of any provisional restoration during healing
questions.explanation: Multiple longitudinal studies and the 2017 World Workshop highlight that inadequate keratinized mucosa and thin soft-tissue phenotype are associated with higher rates of recession, peri-implant mucositis, and patient-reported discomfort. Thick soft tissue also masks underlying metallic or gray hues and stabilizes the mid-facial mucosal level. While cleanability is important, ‘zero PD’ is neither realistic nor required. Abutment material selection and provisionalization timing influence outcomes but are secondary to the soft-tissue volume and quality that were established during the reconstructive phases.

title: Class II Furcation on a Strategic Mandibular Molar — Tunnel, Root Resection or Extraction + Implant?
short: 61M • #30 Class II furcation • 7 mm PD • Strategic abutment for existing FPD

patient.medical_history: Well-controlled hypertension (amlodipine), former smoker (quit 12 years), HbA1c 6.4%. No bisphosphonates or other antiresorptives.
patient.chief_complaint: Food packs between my lower right back teeth and the area bleeds. My dentist said the bone between the roots is gone.

clinical_findings.probing_depths: #30: buccal furcation Class II (Nabers probe penetrates >3 mm but not through-and-through), PD 7 mm at furcation entrance, 5 mm elsewhere. Minimal mobility (Grade 1). Thick phenotype. #31 missing; #30 currently serves as distal abutment for a 3-unit FPD (#28–30).
clinical_findings.radiographs: Vertical bone loss into the furcation, residual inter-radicular bone present, root trunk length approximately 3 mm. No periapical pathology. Adequate bone height apical to the furcation for potential implant placement if extraction chosen.

flags: Class II furcation on strategic abutment
Patient preference for fixed tooth-borne option if predictable
guidelines: 2018 AAP/EFP classification & treatment guidelines
Classic and contemporary furcation management literature (tunnel, root resection, regeneration)
ITI consensus on implant placement in molar sites after extraction

vignette.demographics: 61-year-old male, ASA II, former smoker, well-controlled systemic health. #30 is the distal abutment of an existing 3-unit FPD replacing #29.
vignette.chief: Localized food impaction, bleeding, and concern about the long-term outlook for the molar that supports his bridge.
vignette.clinical: Class II buccal furcation on #30 with 7 mm PD at the entrance. Thick soft tissue, good oral hygiene compliance after initial therapy. Adjacent edentulous span #31. FPD is clinically acceptable but margin on #30 is slightly suboptimal.
vignette.endo: #30 responds normally to vitality testing; no lingering pain or apical findings.
vignette.radio: Moderate vertical bone loss into the buccal furcation. Root trunk ~3 mm. Inter-radicular bone still present. Apical bone sufficient for a standard implant if the tooth is removed.

questions.q: Assuming excellent plaque control after non-surgical therapy, which furcation treatment has the most favorable long-term data for a Class II defect with a short root trunk on a mandibular molar?
options: Regenerative therapy with enamel matrix derivative alone (no bone graft)
Tunnel preparation — provided the patient can maintain inter-radicular hygiene with specific brushes or proxies
Root resection of the distal root and conversion to a single-rooted abutment
No treatment; observe and maintain with 3-month recall only
questions.explanation: For Class II mandibular furcations, tunnel preparation has decades of data showing high retention rates when patients maintain inter-radicular hygiene. A short root trunk actually facilitates tunnel access. Regenerative outcomes in furcations remain less predictable than in contained intrabony defects, especially with short trunks. Root resection is more commonly indicated for Class III or when one root is preferentially compromised, and it converts the tooth into a more complex restorative situation. Pure observation risks further progression in a strategic abutment. Patient dexterity and motivation are prerequisites for the tunnel approach.

questions.q: If the patient elects extraction of #30 and implant replacement, what is the most important pre-extraction counseling point regarding the existing FPD and future prosthesis?
options: The existing FPD can remain in place indefinitely as a cantilever after #30 is removed

Extraction of the distal abutment requires removal of the FPD; the resulting edentulous span (#29–31) will most predictably be restored with two implants or an implant at #30 plus a mesial cantilever only after careful occlusal analysis
An immediate implant at #30 with immediate loading of a new FPD is always the treatment of choice
No implant is needed; a removable partial denture is the standard of care
questions.explanation: Removal of the distal abutment necessitates sectioning or removal of the existing FPD. A distal cantilever on a single implant or on natural teeth carries biomechanical risk, especially in the molar region. Current prosthodontic and implant literature favors either two implants to support a fixed prosthesis or a carefully designed single implant with a short mesial cantilever only when occlusal forces and implant dimensions allow. Immediate loading in a freshly extracted molar socket with peri-implant bone defects is generally avoided. Removable options remain possible but are not the default when fixed solutions are feasible and desired.

questions.q: Which factor most strongly tips the long-term prognosis against retaining #30 via tunneling and toward extraction + implant?
options: Patient age of 61
Presence of a short root trunk combined with an existing restorative margin that violates the biologic width and is not easily correctable
History of former smoking
Thick periodontal phenotype
questions.explanation: A short root trunk already limits the amount of residual attachment after tunneling. When compounded by a restorative margin that invades the biologic width and cannot be corrected without additional crown lengthening (further reducing attachment), the tooth’s long-term maintainability declines sharply. Age and remote smoking history are less decisive once current risk factors are controlled. Thick phenotype is protective, not detrimental. Restorative and periodontal factors must be weighed together when deciding retention versus replacement of a strategic molar.

title: Rapidly Progressive Periodontitis in a Young Adult — Grade C, Microbial Profile & Host Modulation Decisions
short: 29M • Non-smoker • Rapid CAL loss • Family history • Localized angular defects

patient.medical_history: Otherwise healthy, non-smoker, no medications. Mother lost multiple teeth to ‘gum disease’ in her 40s. Recent laboratory values normal (CBC, HbA1c 5.3%).
patient.chief_complaint: My gums have been bleeding and a few teeth shifted in the last 18 months even though I brush twice a day.

clinical_findings.probing_depths: Localized 6–8 mm PDs with angular bone loss on mesial #3, #14, #19, #30. Interproximal CAL 4–6 mm at these sites. Generalized mild inflammation elsewhere. 45% BOP overall. No furcation involvement yet.
clinical_findings.radiographs: Vertical defects 4–6 mm on the mesial surfaces of first molars; remaining dentition shows minimal bone loss. Pattern consistent with molar-incisor or localized rapid progression.

flags: Family history of early tooth loss
Angular defects limited to first molars
Non-smoker, systemically healthy — host susceptibility suspected
guidelines: 2018 AAP/EFP classification (Grade C criteria)
EFP S3 treatment guidelines
Evidence on systemic antibiotics and host-modulation therapy in Grade C periodontitis

vignette.demographics: 29-year-old systemically healthy non-smoking male with a positive family history of early tooth loss. Rapid clinical deterioration noted over 18 months.
vignette.chief: Bleeding gums and shifting of posterior teeth despite reported good home care.
vignette.clinical: Localized deep PDs and angular defects around first molars with CAL 4–6 mm. Generalized mild plaque-induced inflammation. Good overall hygiene compliance after instruction.
vignette.endo: All teeth vital; no endodontic contributions to the angular defects.
vignette.radio: Classic vertical defects on mesial of first molars; remainder of the dentition relatively spared — pattern suggestive of historically ‘localized aggressive’ phenotype now classified as Stage III Grade C.

questions.q: Under the 2018 classification, this presentation is best assigned which Stage and Grade, and why is Grade C appropriate even without longitudinal radiographs?
options: Stage II Grade B — because only first molars are involved
Stage III Grade C — because of the rapid rate of progression inferred from age and severity, plus the molar-incisor pattern historically linked to high-risk profiles
Stage IV Grade C — because mobility is present
Stage III Grade A — because the patient is a non-smoker with normal HbA1c
questions.explanation: Severity (CAL ≥5 mm possible, vertical bone loss) and complexity place the patient at least in Stage III. Grade C is assigned when the percentage of bone loss exceeds expectations for age or when progression is rapid. In a 29-year-old with established angular defects and a family history, the rate is inferred to be rapid even without prior films. The classic molar pattern further supports a high-susceptibility profile. Stage IV requires additional complexity (bite collapse, <20 remaining teeth, etc.). Grade A or B would under-represent the biologic risk.

questions.q: After thorough non-surgical therapy and re-evaluation, what is the current evidence-based position on systemic antibiotics for this Grade C patient?
options: Systemic amoxicillin + metronidazole for 7 days is routinely indicated for every Grade C case regardless of residual disease
Systemic antibiotics may be considered as an adjunct in residual deep sites or specific microbial profiles after mechanical therapy, but are not automatic; decision is individualized
Antibiotics should be given before any instrumentation to suppress A. actinomycetemcomitans
Host-modulation with sub-antimicrobial doxycycline is mandatory and replaces the need for antibiotics
questions.explanation: EFP S3 guidelines do not mandate systemic antibiotics for all Grade C patients. Adjunctive systemic antibiotics (commonly amoxicillin + metronidazole) can provide additional PD reduction and CAL gain in residual deep pockets or in patients with specific microbiologic findings, but the benefit must be weighed against antibiotic stewardship. Pre-instrumentation antibiotics alone are ineffective. Sub-antimicrobial-dose doxycycline is a host-modulation option that may be considered but does not replace mechanical therapy or, when indicated, targeted antimicrobial therapy. The decision remains case-by-case after evaluating residual disease and risk.

questions.q: Long-term maintenance for this patient should emphasize which element most strongly?
options: Annual radiographs only
Strict 3-month supportive periodontal care with targeted instrumentation of residual sites and continuous risk-factor monitoring, because Grade C patients remain at elevated risk of recurrence
Discontinuation of maintenance once PDs are ≤4 mm
Prophylactic extraction of all first molars to prevent future breakdown
questions.explanation: Patients classified as Grade C retain a higher lifetime risk of disease recurrence and progression. Evidence consistently shows that intensive supportive periodontal care (typically every 3 months, customized) is the dominant factor in long-term tooth retention. Radiographs are part of monitoring but insufficient alone. Once stability is achieved, maintenance intensity can be modulated but never discontinued. Pre-emptive extraction of first molars is not supported when the teeth can be retained through regenerative or resective therapy and rigorous maintenance.

title: Immediate Implant in the Esthetic Zone After Extraction of a Periodontally Hopeless Central Incisor — Risk of Recession & Contingency Planning
short: 41F • #8 hopeles s • Thin buccal plate • High smile line • Immediate vs early placement debate

patient.medical_history: Healthy non-smoker, no medications, high esthetic demand, high smile line.
patient.chief_complaint: My front tooth is loose and the gum is receding. I want it replaced as quickly as possible with something that looks natural.

clinical_findings.probing_depths: #8: PD 8–9 mm buccal and mesial, Grade 2 mobility, 3 mm mid-facial recession, thin scalloped phenotype, high smile line exposing gingival margins. Adjacent teeth healthy.
clinical_findings.radiographs: CBCT: severe vertical bone loss on #8, buccal plate thickness <0.5 mm and fenestrated in the coronal third, adequate apical bone (>5 mm) beyond the root apex for primary stability of an immediate implant.

flags: Thin buccal plate + existing mid-facial recession
High smile line / high esthetic risk
Active periodontal infection on the tooth to be extracted
guidelines: ITI Treatment Guide — immediate implant placement in the esthetic zone
2017 World Workshop soft-tissue considerations
Evidence on facial bone thickness and mid-facial recession risk

vignette.demographics: 41-year-old healthy non-smoking female with a high smile line and high esthetic expectations. #8 is periodontally hopeless.
vignette.chief: Request for rapid, natural-looking replacement of a failing maxillary central incisor.
vignette.clinical: Hopeless #8 with deep buccal PD, Grade 2 mobility, and 3 mm mid-facial recession. Thin phenotype and high smile line. Adjacent papillae partially compromised.
vignette.endo: #8 non-vital secondary to advanced periodontal destruction; no acute abscess.
vignette.radio: CBCT confirms near-absence of buccal plate and adequate apical bone for immediate implant anchorage. Vertical hard- and soft-tissue deficiency already present.

questions.q: What is the primary risk of proceeding with immediate implant placement and immediate provisionalization in this specific anatomic situation?
options: Failure to achieve osseointegration because of the periodontal infection
Further mid-facial soft-tissue recession and loss of the buccal contour due to the pre-existing thin/fenestrated buccal plate and thin phenotype
Inability to place the implant in a restoratively driven position
Guaranteed need for systemic antibiotics for 10 days
questions.explanation: The strongest predictor of mid-facial recession after immediate placement is a thin or missing buccal plate combined with a thin soft-tissue phenotype. Pre-existing recession further elevates risk. While primary stability can often be obtained apically and infection can be managed with thorough debridement, the soft-tissue outcome is the dominant esthetic concern in a high-smile-line patient. Restoratively driven positioning is still possible but may require grafting. Antibiotics are sometimes used but are not the central issue.

questions.q: Which alternative timing and sequencing offers the most favorable risk-benefit balance for soft-tissue stability in this high-risk esthetic case?
options: Immediate implant + connective-tissue graft + immediate provisional with maximal facial pressure to ‘support’ the tissue

Atraumatic extraction, ridge preservation (or spontaneous healing with soft-tissue grafting), early or delayed implant placement after soft-tissue maturation, with possible additional contour grafting
Extraction and immediate complete-arch implant rehabilitation to avoid single-tooth soft-tissue problems
Retention of #8 with periodontal surgery and orthodontic extrusion only
questions.explanation: In the presence of a thin/fenestrated buccal plate and pre-existing recession, many experienced clinicians prefer to stage the reconstruction: extract and either preserve or allow controlled healing, augment soft tissue early, then place the implant into a more stable envelope. This reduces the risk of progressive mid-facial recession that is difficult to correct later. Aggressive immediate provisionalization can actually worsen recession if pressure is not perfectly managed. Full-arch conversion is unrelated to the single-site problem. Retention of a hopeless tooth with severe bone loss is not realistic.

questions.q: If immediate placement is still chosen after informed consent, which intraoperative and prosthetic measures most mitigate recession risk?
options: Placing the implant on the facial aspect of the socket to engage residual bone and using a stock healing abutment

Palatal/palato-lingual implant positioning, gap grafting with low-substitution biomaterial, connective-tissue grafting, and a contoured but non-overcontoured provisional that supports but does not pressure the facial mucosa
Leaving the facial gap empty to allow natural blood-clot healing and avoiding any soft-tissue graft
Immediate cement-retained provisional crown with heavy facial contours to ‘plump’ the tissue
questions.explanation: Evidence-based risk mitigation for immediate implants in thin-biotype, deficient-plate sites includes: (1) slightly palatal implant positioning to leave a facial gap, (2) grafting that gap with a slowly resorbing material, (3) soft-tissue augmentation to increase thickness, and (4) a provisional that supports the soft-tissue architecture without excessive facial pressure. Facial positioning worsens recession. Leaving the gap empty or over-contouring the provisional increases the likelihood of mid-facial collapse. These principles are repeatedly emphasized in ITI and contemporary esthetic-zone literature.

title: Complicated Crown Fracture with Pulp Exposure — Mature Apex, 48-Hour Delay
short: 22F • Healthy • #8 complicated crown fracture, 48 h post-trauma, mature apex

patient.medical_history: ASA I. No medications. NKDA. Tetanus up to date.
patient.chief_complaint: I broke my front tooth two days ago playing soccer. It hurts when I breathe in cold air and when I bite.

clinical_findings.probing_depths: Physiologic (<3 mm) around #8; no pathologic pockets.
clinical_findings.mobility: #8 slight mobility (physiologic after trauma); no fremitus.
clinical_findings.radiographs: PA and CBCT: complete root formation, closed apex, no root fracture, no periapical rarefaction, enamel-dentin-pulp exposure ~2 mm diameter on mesio-incisal.

flags: Exposed pulp still vital on testing
guidelines: IADT 2020 Traumatic Dental Injuries Guidelines
AAE Position Statement on Vital Pulp Therapy (2021)
AAE Diagnostic Terminology

vignette.chief: Complicated crown fracture of #8 sustained 48 hours earlier during sports. Sensitivity to cold air and biting.
vignette.clinical: Mesio-incisal fracture exposing ~2 mm of pulp. Soft tissue of lips/ gingiva intact. No alveolar fracture. Tooth slightly mobile but within normal limits post-trauma. Cold testing: lingering response on #8; EPT responsive at higher threshold than contralateral.
vignette.endo: Pulp vital but inflamed. No spontaneous pain. Percussion mild tenderness. No sinus tract.
vignette.radio: Closed apex, intact PDL, no root fracture on PA or limited-FOV CBCT. No apical radiolucency.

questions.q: According to current IADT 2020 and AAE vital-pulp guidelines, what is the most appropriate definitive pulp management for this mature tooth with a 48-hour-old pulp exposure that still responds to vitality testing?
options: Immediate full pulpectomy and root-canal treatment because any exposure older than 24 h in a mature tooth mandates RCT
Partial pulpotomy (or full pulpotomy) with a hydraulic calcium-silicate cement after careful hemorrhage control, followed by definitive adhesive restoration
Direct pulp cap with calcium hydroxide only, without removing inflamed superficial pulp tissue
Extraction and immediate implant because the delay has irreversibly compromised the pulp
questions.explanation: IADT 2020 and the 2021 AAE Vital Pulp Therapy position statement support vital pulp therapy (partial or full pulpotomy) even in mature teeth when the pulp is still vital and the exposure can be managed under aseptic conditions. Hydraulic calcium-silicate cements (MTA, bioceramics) show high success. A rigid 24-hour cutoff for RCT is outdated. Direct pulp capping alone without removing the superficial inflamed tissue has lower success after delayed presentation. Extraction is not indicated.

questions.q: Which of the following is the strongest predictor of success for vital pulp therapy in this scenario?
options: Patient age under 25 years
Ability to achieve hemostasis within 5 minutes after partial pulpotomy and placement of a biocompatible barrier
Use of calcium hydroxide rather than a bioceramic material
Absence of any percussion sensitivity
questions.explanation: Hemostasis within a few minutes after removal of the superficial inflamed pulp is the key clinical indicator that the remaining pulp is healthy enough for VPT. Persistent bleeding suggests more extensive inflammation and lower success. Age is less critical than pulp status once the apex is closed. Bioceramics outperform traditional calcium hydroxide. Mild percussion sensitivity is common after trauma and does not preclude VPT.

questions.q: Red-team / risk-management: If the patient later develops signs of pulp necrosis and apical periodontitis, what is the most important pretreatment imaging and planning step before initiating non-surgical root-canal treatment?
options: A single periapical radiograph is sufficient
Limited-FOV CBCT to rule out undetected root fracture, assess canal morphology, and establish a baseline for healing
Panoramic radiograph only
No further imaging is needed because the original CBCT is still valid
questions.explanation: AAE/AAOMR joint position statements recommend limited-FOV CBCT for traumatic injuries when root fracture or complex anatomy is possible and before retreatment or surgery. It provides critical information that a single PA cannot. Relying solely on the original post-trauma CBCT months later is inadequate for new pathology.

title: Avulsed Permanent Incisor — 75-Minute Extra-Oral Dry Time
short: 16M • Healthy • #9 avulsed, dry storage 75 min, closed apex

patient.medical_history: ASA I. No medications. NKDA. Last tetanus booster 4 years ago.
patient.chief_complaint: My front tooth got knocked out at practice. I found it on the ground and brought it in a paper towel.

clinical_findings.probing_depths: Socket intact; no alveolar fracture clinically.
clinical_findings.radiographs: Socket of #9 empty, no root fragments, closed apex on the avulsed tooth, no other fractures.

guidelines: IADT 2020 Guidelines for Avulsion of Permanent Teeth
AAE Recommended Guidelines for Treatment of Traumatic Dental Injuries

vignette.chief: Avulsion of #9 approximately 75 minutes earlier; tooth transported dry in a paper towel.
vignette.clinical: Empty socket, minimal contamination, no obvious alveolar fracture. Soft-tissue lacerations minor. Tooth has closed apex, periodontal ligament appears desiccated.
vignette.endo: Tooth is non-vital by definition after avulsion with prolonged dry time.
vignette.radio: Empty socket, closed apex on avulsed tooth, no root or alveolar fracture visible on PA.

questions.q: According to IADT 2020, what is the recommended management sequence for this closed-apex avulsed tooth with >60 minutes extra-oral dry time?
options: Replant immediately after rinsing, flexible splint 2 weeks, initiate RCT within 7–10 days, systemic antibiotics optional
Do not replant; the PDL is non-viable and ankylosis/replacement resorption is inevitable, so plan for prosthetic replacement
Replant after soaking in fluoride, rigid splint for 4–6 weeks, delay RCT until symptoms appear
Replant, start RCT immediately extra-orally before replantation, rigid splint 2 months
questions.explanation: IADT 2020 still recommends replantation even after >60 min dry time for closed-apex teeth (to preserve alveolar bone and soft-tissue contour, even if ankylosis is likely). Clean the root and socket, replant, flexible splint for 2 weeks, and commence endodontic treatment within 7–10 days (pulp will necrose). Extra-oral RCT before replantation is no longer preferred. Rigid long-term splinting increases ankylosis risk. While ankylosis is expected, immediate prosthetic replacement discards the chance to maintain the ridge.

questions.q: Which systemic medication consideration is most appropriate per current IADT guidance?
options: No systemic antibiotics are ever indicated for avulsion
Systemic antibiotics (e.g., doxycycline or penicillin) may be considered; tetanus status must be verified and updated if needed
High-dose corticosteroids for 2 weeks to prevent resorption
Antifungal therapy because dry storage guarantees fungal contamination
questions.explanation: IADT 2020 states that systemic antibiotics may be given at the physician’s/dentist’s discretion (evidence is mixed but still commonly used). Tetanus immunization status must always be checked after avulsion. Long-term corticosteroids are not indicated. Antifungals are not part of the protocol.

questions.q: Long-term red-team risk: What is the most likely unfavorable sequela and the appropriate monitoring strategy?
options: Internal resorption only; monitor with annual PA radiographs

Replacement resorption (ankylosis) and eventual infra-occlusion; clinical percussion + radiographic follow-up at 1, 3, 6, 12 months then annually; plan for decoronation or prosthetic replacement when indicated
No long-term sequelae expected if RCT is done promptly
External invasive cervical resorption only; no monitoring needed after the first year
questions.explanation: Prolonged dry time destroys PDL viability → replacement resorption/ankylosis is expected. In a growing patient this leads to infra-occlusion. IADT recommends structured clinical and radiographic follow-up. Decoronation is a recognized option to preserve bone once infra-occlusion becomes significant. Prompt RCT prevents infection-related (inflammatory) resorption but cannot prevent replacement resorption.

title: External Inflammatory Root Resorption after Luxation Injury
short: 19M • #9 prior subluxation • progressive external resorption + pulp necrosis

patient.medical_history: ASA I. History of subluxation of #9 eight months ago; no endodontic treatment performed at that time.
patient.chief_complaint: My front tooth has turned gray and the gum above it feels tender. I thought it was fine after the accident.

clinical_findings.radiographs: PA and CBCT: mid-root external radiolucent defect on the facial aspect of #9, associated with pulp canal space; small apical radiolucency; no root fracture.

guidelines: IADT 2020
AAE Diagnostic Terminology & Resorption Classification
AAE/AAOMR CBCT Position Statement

vignette.chief: Gray discoloration and mild tenderness of #9 eight months after a subluxation injury that was never endodontically treated.
vignette.clinical: Gray crown #9. Negative cold and EPT. Mild percussion tenderness. No sinus tract. Soft tissues otherwise normal.
vignette.endo: Pulp necrosis with symptomatic apical periodontitis and concurrent external inflammatory resorption.
vignette.radio: CBCT confirms external mid-root radiolucent defect communicating with the canal space and a small apical lesion. Remaining dentin thickness is adequate for retention if infection is controlled.

questions.q: The mid-root external resorptive defect in the presence of pulp necrosis is best classified as:
options: Internal replacement resorption
External inflammatory resorption
External cervical (invasive) resorption
Surface resorption only (self-limiting)
questions.explanation: External inflammatory resorption is driven by pulpal infection and typically appears on the root surface adjacent to necrotic pulp tissue. It is progressive until the stimulus (infection) is removed. Internal replacement resorption occurs inside the canal. External cervical resorption is a different entity (usually coronal third, often with vital pulp or different etiology). Surface resorption is shallow and self-limiting.

questions.q: What is the most appropriate immediate endodontic sequence?
options: Observation only; resorption will arrest spontaneously
Thorough chemomechanical debridement, intracanal medicament (calcium hydroxide), then definitive obturation once symptoms resolve; consider internal bleaching after obturation
Immediate extraction because resorption has already doomed the tooth
Regenerative endodontic procedure as first-line therapy in a mature tooth
questions.explanation: Removal of the pulpal infection is the essential first step to arrest external inflammatory resorption. Calcium hydroxide is classically used because of its antibacterial and anti-resorptive properties. Once the canal is disinfected and symptoms resolve, obturation is completed. Internal bleaching can follow. Extraction is not required when sufficient root structure remains. REP is indicated primarily for immature teeth.

questions.q: Which imaging and documentation step is most critical for both treatment planning and long-term follow-up?
options: Periapical radiographs only at yearly intervals
Limited-FOV CBCT at baseline to map the three-dimensional extent of resorption and remaining dentin, then periodic clinical + radiographic review
Panoramic radiograph is sufficient
No further imaging once RCT is completed
questions.explanation: CBCT is the standard of care for mapping resorptive defects, quantifying remaining root structure, and detecting early recurrence. AAE/AAOMR guidance supports its use in trauma-related resorption. Two-dimensional PAs alone underestimate the defect.

title: Cracked Tooth with Pulp Involvement — Restorability Decision
short: 48F • #30 cracked tooth • lingering cold + bite pain • questionable ferrule

patient.chief_complaint: My lower right molar hurts when I bite on hard food and the cold sensitivity lingers for almost a minute.

clinical_findings.probing_depths: 4 mm isolated probing on the facial of #30; otherwise ≤3 mm.
clinical_findings.radiographs: PA: large MOD restoration, subtle vertical radiolucent line suggestion on mesial root; no clear periapical lesion yet. Bitewing confirms deep restoration margins.

guidelines: AAE Cracked Tooth & Vertical Root Fracture resources
AAE Diagnostic Terminology
Prosthodontic ferrule principles

vignette.chief: Bite pain and lingering cold sensitivity on #30.
vignette.clinical: Large MOD amalgam. Pain on release with Tooth Slooth on the mesial cusp. Lingering cold response. Isolated 4 mm facial probing depth. No sinus tract.
vignette.endo: Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis with symptomatic apical periodontitis (early). Crack visible under magnification after removal of restoration, extending into the pulp chamber floor but not clearly onto the external root surface.
vignette.radio: No definitive vertical root fracture on PA; CBCT may be considered if surgical exploration is planned.

questions.q: After confirming the crack extends into the pulp chamber, what is the most appropriate next clinical step before committing to root-canal treatment?
options: Immediate RCT and full-coverage crown without further evaluation of the crack extent

Complete removal of the existing restoration, visualization under magnification/illumination, staining, and transillumination to map the apical and proximal extent of the crack; then decide on restorability
Extraction is mandatory once a crack reaches the pulp
Pulp capping and a new direct restoration because the pulp is only reversibly inflamed
questions.explanation: AAE guidance emphasizes thorough evaluation of crack extent under magnification before treatment decisions. An isolated deep probing or crack that extends apical to the CEJ or onto the root surface markedly worsens prognosis. Jumping straight to RCT without mapping the crack risks treating a non-restorable tooth. Lingering thermal pain indicates irreversible pulpitis, so pulp capping is inappropriate.

questions.q: If the crack is confined to the crown and coronal one-third of the root and a 2 mm ferrule can still be achieved, what is the evidence-based restorative endpoint after RCT?
options: Direct composite only
Full-coverage crown (preferably bonded ceramic or cast restoration) as soon as practical after obturation to cuspal protection
No restoration is needed beyond the access filling
Post and core is always required
questions.explanation: Cuspal coverage is essential for cracked teeth after endodontic treatment to prevent crack propagation. A ferrule of ≥2 mm improves fracture resistance. Posts are used only when retention for the core is insufficient; they are not automatic. Direct composites alone leave the tooth vulnerable to further cracking.

questions.q: Which finding would most strongly shift the plan toward extraction rather than RCT + crown?
options: Mild percussion sensitivity
Isolated probing depth ≥5–6 mm associated with the crack line and radiographic suggestion of the fracture extending onto the root surface
Patient age over 45
Presence of a large existing restoration
questions.explanation: Deep isolated probing and radiographic or clinical evidence that the crack has progressed onto the root surface (vertical root fracture pattern) carry a poor prognosis for tooth retention. Age and restoration size alone are not decisive.

title: Immature Permanent Incisor with Necrotic Pulp & Apical Periodontitis — REP vs Apexification
short: 9F • #8 dens invaginatus • open apex • large apical lesion

patient.chief_complaint: My daughter’s front tooth is discolored and the gum has a pimple that comes and goes.

clinical_findings.probing_depths: Normal; sinus tract on the facial mucosa opposite #8.
clinical_findings.radiographs: PA/CBCT: incomplete root formation, wide-open apex, large periapical radiolucency, dens invaginatus (Oehlers type II) on #8.

guidelines: AAE Clinical Considerations for Regenerative Endodontic Procedures (current)
IADT / AAE trauma and immature-tooth guidance
European Society of Endodontology position on REP

vignette.chief: Discoloration of #8 and intermittent sinus tract.
vignette.clinical: Grayish crown #8. Negative sensibility tests. Facial sinus tract traces to the apex of #8. No caries; dens invaginatus evident clinically and radiographically.
vignette.endo: Necrotic pulp with chronic apical abscess. Open apex (>1–2 mm). Canal walls thin.
vignette.radio: Wide-open apex, thin dentinal walls, large apical radiolucency, invagination extending into the canal.

questions.q: In this immature tooth with a necrotic pulp and apical periodontitis, which statement best reflects current AAE guidance on regenerative endodontic procedures (REP)?
options: REP is contraindicated once a sinus tract is present
REP is a viable first-line option when the goal is continued root development and thickening of canal walls; thorough disinfection and a biocompatible scaffold/seal are required
Apexification with long-term calcium hydroxide is always superior to REP
Immediate extraction and space maintenance is preferred in a 9-year-old
questions.explanation: AAE REP considerations support regenerative approaches for immature teeth with pulp necrosis to allow further root development. Presence of a sinus tract does not contraindicate REP once infection is controlled. Long-term Ca(OH)₂ apexification can weaken roots. Extraction is a last resort in a growing child when the tooth can be retained.

questions.q: What is the most critical disinfection step that differentiates successful REP from traditional apexification?
options: Use of 6 % NaOCl only, without any medicament

Minimal mechanical instrumentation, copious irrigation with NaOCl (lower concentration often preferred), followed by an intracanal medicament (commonly calcium hydroxide or a low-concentration antibiotic paste), then induction of a blood clot or use of a scaffold and a coronal bioceramic seal
Heavy rotary instrumentation to the apex to remove all bacteria
Systemic antibiotics alone without local canal disinfection
questions.explanation: REP protocols emphasize chemical disinfection while preserving remaining stem-cell niches. Heavy mechanical instrumentation is avoided. Calcium hydroxide or dilute antibiotic pastes are used as medicaments. A blood-clot scaffold or alternative scaffold plus a tight coronal seal is required. Systemic antibiotics alone are insufficient.

questions.q: If REP is chosen and the dens invaginatus is present, what additional technical consideration is essential?
options: Ignore the invagination; it will not affect disinfection
Map and disinfect the invagination (often requiring magnification and possible CBCT-guided access) because it can harbor residual biofilm and cause persistent infection
Always extract because dens invaginatus makes REP impossible
Fill the invagination with amalgam before starting REP
questions.explanation: Dens invaginatus creates an additional niche for bacteria. Failure to locate, instrument, and disinfect it is a common cause of REP or conventional treatment failure. Magnification and CBCT are valuable. Extraction is not automatic; many such teeth can be managed endodontically.

title: Persistent Apical Periodontitis after Prior RCT — Retreatment vs Apical Surgery
short: 41M • #19 prior RCT • persistent lesion • separated instrument in MB canal

patient.medical_history: ASA II (well-controlled type 2 diabetes, HbA1c 6.7 %). No allergies.
patient.chief_complaint: I had a root canal on my lower molar two years ago. It still feels pressure when I chew and the X-ray still shows a dark spot.

clinical_findings.probing_depths: All ≤3 mm; no isolated deep pockets.
clinical_findings.radiographs: PA/CBCT: prior RCT #19, separated rotary file in the middle third of the mesial root, 5 mm apical radiolucency involving both mesial and distal roots, no root fracture.

guidelines: AAE Treatment Options for the Compromised Tooth
AAE/AAOMR CBCT guidance for endodontic surgery
Current evidence on non-surgical retreatment vs endodontic microsurgery

vignette.chief: Persistent biting pressure and radiographic lesion two years after RCT on #19.
vignette.clinical: Tooth restored with a well-fitting crown. Mild percussion tenderness. No sinus tract. No deep probing.
vignette.endo: Previously treated tooth with symptomatic apical periodontitis. Separated instrument visible in mesial root.
vignette.radio: CBCT confirms the separated file location, size of the osteolytic lesion, and absence of root fracture or significant bone loss that would preclude surgery.

questions.q: What is the most appropriate first-line approach according to current evidence when both non-surgical retreatment and apical microsurgery are technically feasible?
options: Immediate extraction and implant because any separated instrument dooms the tooth

Non-surgical orthograde retreatment (attempting instrument bypass or removal) when access through the crown is possible and the canal system can be re-disinfected; microsurgery reserved for cases in which retreatment is not feasible or fails
Apical surgery first in every case with a separated instrument
Long-term observation only; many lesions heal spontaneously after two years
questions.explanation: Evidence and AAE guidance favor non-surgical retreatment as the first option when the canal system is accessible and the goal is to improve disinfection. Separated instruments can often be bypassed or removed with modern techniques. Microsurgery is highly successful but is generally considered after, or when, orthograde revision is not practical. Observation of a symptomatic lesion with a known instrument is not appropriate.

questions.q: If non-surgical retreatment is unsuccessful or the separated file cannot be safely managed orthograde, which statement about modern endodontic microsurgery is correct?
options: Traditional rotary surgery without magnification has the same success rate as microsurgery

Endodontic microsurgery (magnification, ultrasonic root-end preparation, biocompatible root-end fillings) achieves high success rates (often >90 % in selected cases) and is a predictable alternative to extraction
Microsurgery is contraindicated in patients with controlled diabetes
Root-end resection of 1 mm is sufficient regardless of anatomy
questions.explanation: Contemporary microsurgical techniques have markedly improved outcomes compared with traditional surgery. Controlled diabetes is not a contraindication. Root-end resection of approximately 3 mm is generally recommended to remove most lateral canals and apical ramifications; 1 mm is usually insufficient.

questions.q: Red-team decision point: Which factor would most strongly favor extraction and implant rather than further endodontic efforts?
options: Patient preference for a long-term, low-maintenance solution combined with radiographic evidence of a vertical root fracture or insufficient remaining tooth structure for a reliable ferrule
Presence of a separated instrument alone
Lesion size >4 mm
History of one prior RCT
questions.explanation: A confirmed vertical root fracture or inability to achieve a restorative ferrule are classic indications to move to extraction. A separated instrument, lesion size, or single prior RCT are not by themselves absolute indications for extraction when modern retreatment or microsurgery remains feasible.
